passages.s: What would exceed the rigour of this severity?

And so it is not so much the aspect of this place which moves me, as thy aspect; not so much the library walls set off with glass and ivory which I miss, as the chamber of thy mind, wherein I once placed, not books, but that which gives books their value, the doctrines which my books contain.
But it is time for thee to take and drain a draught, soft and pleasant to the taste, which, as it penetrates within, may prepare the way for stronger potions.
What if not even now have I departed wholly from thee?
Wherefore, it is not easy for anyone to be at perfect peace with the circumstances of his lot.
From all which 'tis plainly proved that not one of these things which thou reckonest in the number of thy possessions is really thine.

And yet wealth cannot extinguish insatiable greed, nor has power ever made him master of himself whom vicious lusts kept bound in indissoluble fetters; dignity conferred on the wicked not only fails to make them worthy, but contrarily reveals and displays their unworthiness.
What to leaguèd peace hath bent Every warring element?
And as for bodily excellences, it is obvious that they are to be ranged with the above.

Why, the prefecture, which was once a great power, is now an empty name--a burden merely on the senator's fortune; the commissioner of the public corn supply was once a personage--now what is more contemptible than this office?
This is the way of Pleasure: She stings them that despoil her; And, like the wingéd toiler Who's lost her honeyed treasure, She flies, but leaves her smart Deep-rankling in the heart.

So if there is, as we showed before, a happiness of a frail and imperfect kind, it cannot be doubted but there is also a happiness substantial and perfect.' 'Most true is thy conclusion, and most sure,' said I.
And we are not now treating of the voluntary motions of an intelligent soul, but of the drift of nature.
Thus all fortune is good fortune; for it either rewards, disciplines, amends, or punishes, and so is either useful or just.
But it was agreed that those who are happy are gods.
No right nor reason can they show; 'Tis but because their lands and laws are not the same.

Some, through a prosperity unworthily borne, have been hurled headlong to ruin; to some the power of the sword has been committed, to the end that the good may be tried by discipline, and the bad punished.
If we could know, as He knows, all that is most perplexing in this problem would be made plain.
We can obviously reason similarly in the case of providence and the future.
But this, thou wilt say, is the very point in dispute--whether any foreknowing is possible of things whose occurrence is not necessary.
